description: A complete 60-day Swedish A1 course presented one day at a time. Each lesson includes Swedish-English phrases, a short dialogue, grammar support, and practice tasks.

days.title: Alphabet, pronunciation, greetings
days.goal: Learn Swedish letters Å, Ä, Ö, basic pronunciation, greetings, polite words, and a simple “How are you?” dialogue.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: Start the course by learning the extra Swedish letters, greeting people politely, and answering a simple question about how you feel.

table.English: you are welcome / here you go
table.Example English: Here you go, the coffee is ready.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Swedish often says “Jag mår bra” for “I am fine.” Literally it means “I feel well,” so do not replace it with “Jag är bra.”

table.Approx sound: round your lips and say e

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.swedish: Jag mår bra, tack. Och du?
dialogue.english: I am fine, thanks. And you?

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Say “Hej” and “Hejdå” five times.
Practice “Hur mår du?” slowly, then at natural speed.
Answer with “Jag mår bra, tack.”
Read the mini-dialogue aloud twice.

vocabulary.english: you are welcome / here you go
vocabulary.exampleEnglish: Here you go, the coffee is ready.

days.title: Saying your name and where you are from
days.goal: Introduce yourself, say your name, and tell someone where you are from.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: Today you build your first self-introduction in Swedish: your name, your country, and a simple question back to the other person.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: “Jag heter” means “my name is.” To say where you are from, use “Jag kommer från ...” or “Jag är från ...” in simple beginner speech.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Say your full introduction aloud three times.
Replace the country with your own country.
Ask “Varifrån kommer du?” and answer it.
Write two short introduction lines about yourself.

days.title: Classroom phrases and polite requests
days.goal: Use basic classroom Swedish to ask for repetition, help, and clarification.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: This lesson gives you survival Swedish for learning: asking someone to repeat, saying you do not understand, and asking what a word means.

table.Example English: What does that mean in English?

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: “Kan du ...?” means “Can you ...?” and is a useful polite frame for requests. “Jag förstår inte” means “I do not understand.”

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Practice “Jag förstår inte” without translating in your head.
Ask for repetition politely three times.
Choose one Swedish word and ask what it means.
Read the dialogue with a pause after each line.

vocabulary.exampleEnglish: What does that mean in English?

days.title: Numbers 0-20, age, and phone numbers
days.goal: Count from 0 to 20, say your age, and read simple numbers aloud.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: Today you train Swedish numbers so you can say your age and begin hearing number patterns clearly.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: To say your age, Swedish uses “Jag är ... år.” The word “år” means “years old” in this context.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Count from 0 to 20 twice.
Say your age in Swedish three times.
Read a phone number digit by digit.
Test yourself by covering the English column.

days.title: Countries, languages, and nationalities
days.goal: Name a few countries, languages, and nationalities in Swedish.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: You will connect country names with the languages people speak and practice short identity sentences.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: After “Jag talar ...” use the language name, for example “Jag talar engelska.” Nationalities often change form depending on gender and number, so start by recognizing them.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Jag talar engelska och lite svenska.
dialogue.english: I speak English and a little Swedish.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Say three languages you know or study.
Make one sentence with “Jag talar ...”.
Practice “lite svenska” for natural rhythm.
Read the dialogue until it feels smooth.

days.title: Subject pronouns
days.goal: Use the subject pronouns jag, du, han, hon, vi, ni, and de.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: You are learning the basic people-words that appear in nearly every sentence in Swedish.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Swedish subject pronouns usually stay before the verb in simple statements: “Jag bor här.” “Hon studerar.”

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Read the pronouns aloud as a chain: jag, du, han, hon, vi, ni, de.
Make one sentence with “jag” and one with “vi”.
Switch a sentence from “jag” to “du”.
Listen to your own pronunciation while reading the dialogue.

days.title: Verb är: to be
days.goal: Use the verb är in basic statements and questions.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: This lesson gives you one of the most important verbs in Swedish so you can describe identity, location, and simple facts.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: The present form is “är” for all persons: jag är, du är, vi är. Swedish does not change it like English does with am / is / are.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.english: A little, but I am fine.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Make three “Jag är ...” sentences.
Ask one yes/no question with “Är du ...?”
Replace “student” with your own role.
Read the dialogue with clear stress on “är”.

days.title: Simple sentence order
days.goal: Build short Swedish statements with subject + verb + extra information.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: You now practice the default Swedish word order so your beginner sentences sound stable and clear.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: A safe beginner pattern is subject + verb + object/place/time: “Jag läser svenska hemma.” Keep that pattern until it feels automatic.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: What do you do every day?

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Write two sentences using subject + verb + place.
Say one sentence with “varje dag”.
Swap the verb in the model sentence.
Read the dialogue and notice the basic order.

days.title: Questions: what, who, where
days.goal: Ask and answer basic information questions.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: You will use question words to keep a conversation going instead of only answering yes or no.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Common question words are “vad” (what), “vem” (who), and “var” (where). In simple questions the verb usually comes before the subject.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Ask one question with “vad”, one with “vem”, and one with “var”.
Answer using full sentences, not single words.
Practice “Var bor du?” at natural speed.
Read the dialogue aloud with correct question intonation.

days.title: Review and speaking practice
days.goal: Review Days 1-9 and combine greetings, introductions, and basic questions.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: This is the first consolidation day. You will recycle earlier material into one longer beginner conversation.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Review days matter because A1 progress comes from reusing the same structures until they become quick and familiar.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.swedish: Hej! Jag heter Sara. Vad heter du?
dialogue.english: Hi! My name is Sara. What is your name?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Jag heter Amir. Jag kommer från Iran.
dialogue.english: My name is Amir. I come from Iran.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Jag bor i Stockholm och jag talar lite svenska.
dialogue.english: I live in Stockholm and I speak a little Swedish.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Introduce yourself for 30 seconds without looking.
Ask and answer three questions from earlier days.
Repeat one line until you can say it smoothly.
Record yourself if possible and listen back once.

days.title: Family words
days.goal: Talk about close family members and ask simple family questions.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: Today you learn the most common family words so you can describe the people around you.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: To ask “Do you have ...?” use “Har du ...?” and answer with “Ja, jag har ...” or “Nej, jag har inte ...”.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Say four family words aloud.
Make one sentence with “min mamma” and one with “min pappa”.
Answer “Har du syskon?” with a full sentence.
Read the dialogue and replace the city with your own.

days.title: Possessives: my, your, his, her
days.goal: Use possessive words to talk about people and things that belong to someone.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: You are learning to attach ownership to nouns, which makes your Swedish much more personal and precise.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Common possessives are “min / mitt / mina” for my and “din / ditt / dina” for your. At this stage, recognize the forms and use common chunks like “min familj”.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Point at three objects and say “min ...” or “din ...”.
Say one example with “hans” and one with “hennes”.
Answer the dialogue without reading the English.
Notice that possessives come before the noun.

days.title: Jobs and studies
days.goal: Say what you do, where you study, or what kind of work you have.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: This lesson helps you answer one of the most common small-talk questions: what you do.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Use “Jag är ...” for professions in simple introductions and “Jag studerar ...” or “Jag jobbar som ...” for more detail.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Ja, jag är student på kvällstid.
dialogue.english: Yes, I am a student in the evenings.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Say your own work or study sentence three times.
Practice “Jag jobbar som ...”.
Ask someone “Vad jobbar du med?”
Read the dialogue and switch the profession.

days.title: Common verbs in present tense
days.goal: Use a small set of common present-tense verbs in short sentences.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: You are moving from fixed phrases toward flexible sentence building with common everyday verbs.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: In the present tense, many Swedish verbs end in -r: bor, läser, skriver, talar. Learn them as whole forms first.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Ja, jag dricker kaffe varje morgon.
dialogue.english: Yes, I drink coffee every morning.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Lite grann, jag skriver enkla meningar.
dialogue.english: A little, I write simple sentences.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Make one sentence with each verb.
Read the verbs aloud and notice the final -r sound.
Ask two yes/no questions using the verbs.
Rebuild the dialogue with your own answers.

days.title: Likes and dislikes
days.goal: Say what you like and do not like in Swedish.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: Today you add opinions to your Swedish so you can talk about food, hobbies, and language learning preferences.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Use “Jag gillar ...” for “I like ...” and “Jag gillar inte ...” for “I do not like ...”. The negation comes after the verb.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.english: No, I do not like tea.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Say three things you like.
Say two things you do not like.
Practice the difference between “gillar” and “gillar inte”.
Answer the dialogue with your real preferences.

days.title: Food and drinks
days.goal: Recognize and use common food and drink words in short sentences.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: This vocabulary lesson prepares you for cafés, restaurants, and everyday talk about meals.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: When naming food in basic speech, short noun phrases are enough: “en kaffe” is common in cafés, although “en kopp kaffe” is more literal.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Jag vill ha kaffe och bröd.
dialogue.english: I would like coffee and bread.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Name four food or drink items from memory.
Say “Jag vill ha ...” with two different items.
Ask for water politely.
Read the café dialogue twice.

days.title: Ordering in a café
days.goal: Order simple items in a café and understand basic service phrases.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: You will combine food vocabulary with polite requests in a realistic café exchange.

table.Example Swedish: Jag skulle vilja ha en kaffe.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: A very useful pattern is “Jag skulle vilja ha ...” for a polite “I would like ...”, but “Jag vill ha ...” is acceptable at beginner level.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.swedish: Hej, vad får det lov att vara?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Jag skulle vilja ha en kaffe utan socker.
dialogue.english: I would like a coffee without sugar.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Ja, kan jag få notan senare?
dialogue.english: Yes, can I get the bill later?

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Order one drink and one snack aloud.
Practice “utan” with sugar or milk.
Ask for the bill politely.
Read the dialogue and play both roles.

vocabulary.exampleSwedish: Jag skulle vilja ha en kaffe.

days.title: en and ett nouns
days.goal: Recognize the two Swedish noun genders and use them in simple phrases.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: Swedish nouns are often learned with en or ett. This lesson helps you treat the article as part of the word.

table.Example English: The book is on a table.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: There is no perfect rule for en and ett at A1 level, so memorize common noun phrases like “en bok” and “ett hus.”

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Det är ett bord och en stol.
dialogue.english: It is a table and a chair.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Read each noun together with en or ett.
Make two sentences with object words around you.
Do not memorize the noun without its article.
Use the dialogue as a pointing exercise in your room.

vocabulary.exampleEnglish: The book is on a table.

days.title: Plurals introduction
days.goal: Recognize and use a few common plural forms.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: You are taking the first step into Swedish plural nouns so you can talk about more than one thing.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Swedish plural patterns vary, so begin with high-frequency pairs such as bok / böcker and stol / stolar.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: How many books do you have?

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Say singular and plural pairs aloud.
Make one sentence with a number and one plural noun.
Practice “många” with two different nouns.
Read the dialogue and stress the plural endings.

days.title: Review and roleplay
days.goal: Review family, food, and noun basics with short roleplays.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: This review day mixes people, objects, and café language so you can start switching topics naturally.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Roleplay is useful because it forces you to retrieve language quickly instead of only recognizing it.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.swedish: Vad vill du ha på kaféet?
dialogue.english: What would you like at the café?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Jag skulle vilja ha kaffe och bröd.
dialogue.english: I would like coffee and bread.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Do a one-minute self-introduction from memory.
Ask three questions from previous lessons.
Roleplay a café or classroom exchange.
Repeat weak vocabulary aloud five times.

days.title: Days of the week
days.goal: Say the days of the week and talk about simple weekly routines.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: You will learn calendar vocabulary that helps you speak about plans, work, and study habits.

table.Example English: I work at home on Friday.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: To say “on Monday” Swedish often uses just the day word in context, but “på måndag” means “on Monday / this coming Monday.”

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Jag studerar på måndag och onsdag.
dialogue.english: I study on Monday and Wednesday.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: What do you do on Friday?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Jag jobbar och sedan vilar jag på helgen.
dialogue.english: I work and then I rest on the weekend.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Say all seven days in order.
Describe your study days in Swedish.
Practice “på måndag” and “på fredag”.
Read the dialogue and replace the days.

vocabulary.exampleEnglish: I work at home on Friday.

days.title: Months and dates
days.goal: Recognize common month names and say simple dates.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: Today you build calendar control so you can speak about birthdays, meetings, and seasons.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Dates in Swedish are often said with ordinal-like forms in speech, but at A1 level it is fine to recognize and read simple dates slowly.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: What is the date of the meeting?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.english: It is on the twelfth of August.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Say three months that matter to you.
Practice asking for today’s date.
Read a sample date slowly and clearly.
Repeat the dialogue and change the month.

days.title: Telling time
days.goal: Ask for and say simple times in Swedish.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: You need time language for meetings, classes, transport, and daily routine questions.

table.Example English: It is half past two / half to three in Swedish style.
The lesson starts at nine o’clock.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: A practical beginner structure is “Klockan är ...” for “The time is ...” and “När börjar ...?” for asking when something starts.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.english: It is half past two / Swedish half three.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Practice full hours first, then half hours.
Ask “Vad är klockan?” three times.
Say when your lesson or work starts.
Read the dialogue and focus on “halv”.

vocabulary.exampleEnglish: It is half past two / half to three in Swedish style.
The lesson starts at nine o’clock.

days.title: Daily routine
days.goal: Describe your day using common routine verbs.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: This lesson lets you speak about waking up, working, eating, and sleeping in simple sequence.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: To describe routine, combine time words with present verbs: “Jag vaknar klockan sju. Sedan äter jag frukost.”

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Jag vaknar klockan sju och äter frukost.
dialogue.english: I wake up at seven and eat breakfast.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Describe your morning in three sentences.
Use one time expression in each sentence.
Practice “sedan” silently between actions if it helps sequencing.
Read the dialogue with your real routine.

days.title: Shopping vocabulary
days.goal: Use basic shopping words for clothes, sizes, and buying things.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: You will learn how to identify things in a shop and ask basic questions about them.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Polite shopping questions often begin with “Har ni ...?” meaning “Do you have ...?” when talking to a shop assistant.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Ja, jag vill köpa en tröja.
dialogue.english: Yes, I want to buy a sweater.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Name three things you might buy.
Ask a shop if they have your size.
Practice “Jag vill köpa ...”.
Read the dialogue like a real shop exchange.

days.title: Prices and money
days.goal: Ask about prices and understand simple money language.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: Price questions are essential for shops, cafés, and transport. This lesson gives you the minimum set.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Use “Hur mycket kostar det?” for “How much does it cost?” Swedish currency is kronor, often spoken as “kronor” or “spänn” informally.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: How much does the sweater cost?

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: Okay, it is a little expensive.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Ask about the price of two imaginary items.
Say one item is cheap and one is expensive.
Practice the word “kronor”.
Read the dialogue and replace the item name.

days.title: Asking for help
days.goal: Ask for help politely in public places.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: This lesson gives you useful emergency and support language for everyday situations.

table.Example English: Excuse me, can you help me?
I am looking for the station.
Can you show me the way?

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: A strong survival frame is “Kan du hjälpa mig?” meaning “Can you help me?” Add “ursäkta” first to sound polite.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: Excuse me, can you help me?

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: I am looking for the station.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.english: I can show you the way.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Practice the full help request slowly and clearly.
Replace “stationen” with another place.
Say one sentence with “Jag har ett problem.”
Read the dialogue and switch roles.

vocabulary.exampleEnglish: Excuse me, can you help me?
I am looking for the station.
Can you show me the way?

days.title: Directions and places in town
days.goal: Understand and give simple directions in a town.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: You will learn place words and directional language useful for maps, streets, and asking for locations.

table.Example English: The station is near the center.
The library is on the left.

table.Example Swedish: Gå rakt fram i två minuter.
table.Example English: Go straight ahead for two minutes.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Common direction phrases are “till höger” (to the right), “till vänster” (to the left), and “rakt fram” (straight ahead).

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Gå rakt fram och sväng till höger.
dialogue.english: Go straight ahead and turn right.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Point and say right, left, and straight ahead.
Give directions from your home to one nearby place.
Practice “Var ligger ...?”
Read the dialogue and follow the route with your hand.

vocabulary.exampleEnglish: The station is near the center.
The library is on the left.

vocabulary.exampleSwedish: Gå rakt fram i två minuter.
vocabulary.exampleEnglish: Go straight ahead for two minutes.

days.title: Transport vocabulary
days.goal: Talk about buses, trains, tickets, and simple travel plans.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: Transport language helps you move independently and understand basic travel conversations.

table.Example English: I take the bus to work.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: To say how you travel, use “Jag åker ...” plus transport: “Jag åker buss.” “Jag åker tåg.”

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: How do you get to town?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.english: Yes, but the train departs soon.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Say how you travel to one place.
Ask for a ticket in Swedish.
Practice “avgår snart”.
Read the dialogue and replace bus with train.

vocabulary.exampleEnglish: I take the bus to work.

days.title: Review and mini test
days.goal: Review time, routines, shopping, and transport with short recall tasks.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: This review day checks how well you can switch between routine language and outside-the-home situations.

table.Example English: I try to remember the words.

table.Example Swedish: Idag gör vi ett litet test.
table.Example English: Today we do a small test.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: At this stage, fluency comes from recall speed. Short self-tests are more useful than rereading everything passively.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.swedish: Är du redo för ett litet test?
dialogue.english: Are you ready for a small test?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.english: Yes, I am trying to remember everything.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: How do you get to work?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.english: I take the bus at eight.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Answer ten old questions without opening previous days.
Describe one weekday routine.
Roleplay a shop or transport situation.
Repeat weak answers until they come quickly.

vocabulary.exampleEnglish: I try to remember the words.

vocabulary.exampleSwedish: Idag gör vi ett litet test.
vocabulary.exampleEnglish: Today we do a small test.

days.title: Present tense verbs
days.goal: Strengthen your control of present tense with more frequent verbs.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: You already know some present-tense verbs. Today you expand that set so you can talk more freely.

table.Example English: We are watching the film tonight.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Keep learning verbs as ready-to-use present forms first. Later you can study infinitives and verb classes in more detail.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Ja, och jag ser tavlan också.
dialogue.english: Yes, and I see the board too.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Make one sentence with each verb.
Ask one question using “går” and one using “ser”.
Notice that these verbs are short but common.
Read the dialogue and personalize the travel answer.

vocabulary.exampleEnglish: We are watching the film tonight.

days.title: Word order in statements
days.goal: Practice stable word order in simple Swedish statements.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: Today you train the backbone of Swedish sentences so your statements stay natural when they get longer.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: A strong beginner default is time or subject first, then the verb in second position: “Idag studerar jag svenska.” “Jag studerar svenska idag.”

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Start three sentences with a time word.
Keep the verb near the beginning of the sentence.
Say one sentence with “ibland”.
Read the dialogue and pay attention to verb position.

days.title: Word order in questions
days.goal: Build yes/no questions and information questions more confidently.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: You are practicing the switch that happens in Swedish questions, where the verb often comes before the subject.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Compare “Du bor här.” with “Bor du här?” For question-word questions, the question word comes first: “Var bor du?”

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: För att jag vill jobba här.
dialogue.english: Because I want to work here.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Convert three statements into questions.
Ask one question with each model pattern.
Practice “Varför ...?” with your own reason.
Read the dialogue and feel the question rhythm.

days.title: Negation with inte
days.goal: Use inte correctly in simple sentences and answers.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: Negation is essential for clear communication. Today you practice saying what is not true or what you do not do.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: In simple statements, “inte” usually comes after the verb: “Jag bor inte här.” “Jag gillar inte kaffe.”

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.english: No, I do not live here.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Nej, jag har ingen biljett ännu.
dialogue.english: No, I do not have a ticket yet.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Negate four earlier positive sentences.
Practice the position of “inte” after the verb.
Say one sentence with “aldrig”.
Read the dialogue and emphasize the negative word.

days.title: Adjectives
days.goal: Use basic adjectives to describe people, objects, and situations.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: You are adding descriptive power to your Swedish with common beginner adjectives.

table.Example Swedish: Jag bor i en liten lägenhet.
table.Example English: I live in a small apartment.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: At A1 level, start with common adjective chunks and pay attention to frequent forms in context rather than memorizing every agreement rule immediately.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Describe three objects around you.
Use one adjective for something positive and one for something negative.
Practice the pair stor / liten.
Read the dialogue and replace the noun.

vocabulary.exampleSwedish: Jag bor i en liten lägenhet.
vocabulary.exampleEnglish: I live in a small apartment.

days.title: Describing people and things
days.goal: Describe appearance, personality, and everyday objects using simple adjectives.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: This lesson expands adjective use from objects to people and common descriptions.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Short two-part descriptions are enough at A1 level: “Hon är snäll.” “Det är en fin bok.” Build confidence before adding complexity.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Ibland, men den är också fin.
dialogue.english: Sometimes, but it is also beautiful.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Describe one person and one place.
Use two adjectives in the same sentence.
Practice “ibland svår” naturally.
Read the dialogue and replace the teacher with another person.

days.title: Prepositions
days.goal: Use simple location prepositions in everyday sentences.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: Prepositions help you explain where things are, which is essential in the home, city, and classroom.

table.Example English: The book is on the table.
The keys are in the bag.
The cat sleeps under the chair.
The school is next to the library.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Start with a few high-frequency location words: på (on), i (in), under (under), bredvid (next to).

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: De är i väskan bredvid stolen.
dialogue.english: They are in the bag next to the chair.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Describe where four objects are in your room.
Practice the difference between “på” and “i”.
Make one sentence with “bredvid”.
Read the dialogue while looking around a real room.

vocabulary.exampleEnglish: The book is on the table.
The keys are in the bag.
The cat sleeps under the chair.
The school is next to the library.

days.title: Modal verbs
days.goal: Use can, must, want to, and may in simple statements.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: Modal verbs let you speak about ability, obligation, and desire, which makes your Swedish much more functional.

table.Example English: I can speak a little Swedish.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: After a modal verb like “kan”, “vill”, or “måste”, the next verb stays in the infinitive: “Jag kan tala.” “Jag vill gå.”

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Ja, men jag måste gå snart.
dialogue.english: Yes, but I have to go soon.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.swedish: Får jag fråga en sak först?
dialogue.english: May I ask one thing first?

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Make one sentence with each modal verb.
Use an infinitive after every modal.
Ask permission with “Får jag ...?”
Read the dialogue and emphasize the modal verbs.

vocabulary.exampleEnglish: I can speak a little Swedish.

days.title: Talking about plans
days.goal: Use simple future language to talk about what you are going to do.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: This lesson prepares you for invitations, schedules, and short future plans.

table.Example English: I am going to study tonight.
We are going to cook this evening.
She is going to travel tomorrow.

table.Example Swedish: Vad är din plan för helgen?
table.Example English: What is your plan for the weekend?

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: A practical beginner future form is “ska” + infinitive: “Jag ska studera.” It often means “am going to.”

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: What are you going to do this evening?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.english: I am going to study Swedish.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Imorgon ska jag träffa en vän.
dialogue.english: Tomorrow I am going to meet a friend.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Say your plan for tonight and tomorrow.
Practice “ska” + verb as one chunk.
Ask someone about their weekend plan.
Read the dialogue and swap in your own activities.

vocabulary.exampleEnglish: I am going to study tonight.
We are going to cook this evening.
She is going to travel tomorrow.

vocabulary.exampleSwedish: Vad är din plan för helgen?
vocabulary.exampleEnglish: What is your plan for the weekend?

days.title: Review and writing practice
days.goal: Review grammar control from Days 31-39 and write short personal sentences.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: This day combines verbs, questions, negation, adjectives, prepositions, and simple future plans in short writing tasks.

table.Example English: I am trying to write in Swedish.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Writing reveals gaps that speaking can hide. Keep your sentences short and correct rather than long and confusing.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.english: Yes, I am going to try.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Inte alla, men jag lär mig.
dialogue.english: Not all of them, but I am learning.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Write five short personal sentences.
Include one negative sentence and one future sentence.
Read your own writing aloud once.
Rewrite any sentence that feels unstable.

vocabulary.exampleEnglish: I am trying to write in Swedish.

days.title: At the supermarket
days.goal: Use basic shopping language for food, quantities, and finding items in a supermarket.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: You are moving into real-world errands with useful words for daily shopping.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: A practical pattern is “Var finns ...?” meaning “Where is ...?” Use it when you cannot find an item.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: Excuse me, where is the milk?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Den finns längst bak i butiken.
dialogue.english: It is at the back of the store.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.swedish: Tack. Kan jag få kvittot också?
dialogue.english: Thanks. Can I get the receipt too?

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Name five food items you buy often.
Ask where an item is in a store.
Practice asking for a receipt.
Read the supermarket dialogue twice.

days.title: At a restaurant
days.goal: Order food, ask for recommendations, and make short restaurant requests.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: You already practiced café language. Now you expand it to full meal situations.

table.Example English: I am ordering a main course.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: At A1 level, short requests are fine: “Jag tar ...” or “Jag skulle vilja ha ...” both work in restaurants.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Ja, vi har en vegetarisk huvudrätt.
dialogue.english: Yes, we have a vegetarian main course.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Ask for a vegetarian option.
Use “Vad rekommenderar du?” naturally.
Order a starter or main course aloud.
Read the dialogue and change the food choice.

vocabulary.exampleEnglish: I am ordering a main course.

days.title: At the doctor
days.goal: Use very basic health language to describe common problems.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: This lesson gives you simple, high-value phrases for health situations without trying to cover advanced medical Swedish.

table.Example Swedish: Jag tror att jag har feber.
table.Example English: I think I have a fever.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: To describe pain, use “Jag har ont i ...” meaning “I have pain in ...” or “my ... hurts.”

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Jag har ont i huvudet och jag har feber.
dialogue.english: I have a headache and I have a fever.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.swedish: Hur länge har du varit sjuk?
dialogue.english: How long have you been ill?

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Practice “Jag har ont i ...” with two body parts.
Say whether you have fever or not.
Ask if medicine is needed.
Read the doctor dialogue calmly and clearly.

vocabulary.exampleSwedish: Jag tror att jag har feber.
vocabulary.exampleEnglish: I think I have a fever.

days.title: Weather
days.goal: Describe simple weather conditions and react to them.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: Weather is frequent small-talk material and also useful for planning your day.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: A common structure is “Det är ...” followed by the weather adjective or condition: “Det är kallt.” “Det regnar.”

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Det är soligt men lite kallt.
dialogue.english: It is sunny but a little cold.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Describe the weather today in two sentences.
Use both positive and negative weather words.
Practice “Det är ...” with three adjectives.
Read the dialogue and replace the weather.

days.title: Hobbies
days.goal: Talk about simple hobbies and free-time activities.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: This lesson helps you share interests and understand common social conversation topics.

table.Example Swedish: Hon tränar tre gånger i veckan.
table.Example English: She exercises three times a week.
What do you do in your free time?

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Many hobby sentences use the present tense: “Jag spelar ...” “Jag läser ...” “Jag tränar ...”. Keep them short.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: What do you do in your free time?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Jag gillar att läsa och träna.
dialogue.english: I like to read and exercise.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Say two hobbies you enjoy.
Ask someone about their free time.
Practice “Jag gillar att ...”.
Read the dialogue and replace the hobbies.

vocabulary.exampleSwedish: Hon tränar tre gånger i veckan.
vocabulary.exampleEnglish: She exercises three times a week.
What do you do in your free time?

days.title: Invitations
days.goal: Invite someone to do something at a simple time and place.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: You will use question forms and future language to invite someone politely.

table.Example English: Do you want to have coffee tomorrow?

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: A very useful pattern is “Vill du ...?” meaning “Do you want to ...?” Add a time or place after it.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: Do you want to have coffee tomorrow?

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.swedish: Ska vi träffas i stan klockan sex?
dialogue.english: Shall we meet in town at six?

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Invite someone to coffee, a walk, or a meal.
Accept using “Ja, gärna!”
Set a time and place in Swedish.
Read the dialogue and swap the activity.

vocabulary.exampleEnglish: Do you want to have coffee tomorrow?

days.title: Accepting and declining
days.goal: Accept or decline invitations politely.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: This lesson gives you social control: saying yes clearly and saying no politely with a reason.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: A simple declining structure is “Tyvärr, jag kan inte ...” meaning “Unfortunately, I cannot ...”.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.swedish: Vill du följa med på bio?
dialogue.english: Do you want to come to the cinema?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.english: Unfortunately, I am busy this evening.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Accept one invitation and decline one politely.
Give a short reason when you decline.
Practice “en annan gång”.
Read the dialogue and switch who says no.

days.title: Describing your home
days.goal: Talk about rooms, furniture, and simple home descriptions.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: You will use room vocabulary and adjectives to describe where you live.

table.Example English: The kitchen is small but nice.

table.Example Swedish: Det finns en soffa i vardagsrummet.
table.Example English: There is a sofa in the living room.

table.Example Swedish: Jag bor i en liten lägenhet.
table.Example English: I live in a small apartment.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Useful frames are “Jag bor i ...” and “Det finns ...” for describing what is in your home.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: Do you have a big kitchen?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Nej, men jag har en fin soffa i vardagsrummet.
dialogue.english: No, but I have a nice sofa in the living room.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Describe your home in three sentences.
Name two rooms and two pieces of furniture.
Use “Det finns ...” at least once.
Read the dialogue and change the home type.

vocabulary.exampleEnglish: The kitchen is small but nice.

vocabulary.exampleSwedish: Det finns en soffa i vardagsrummet.
vocabulary.exampleEnglish: There is a sofa in the living room.

vocabulary.exampleSwedish: Jag bor i en liten lägenhet.
vocabulary.exampleEnglish: I live in a small apartment.

days.title: Travel and hotel basics
days.goal: Use simple Swedish for check-in, hotel questions, and travel needs.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: This lesson covers very practical beginner travel phrases that are useful immediately.

table.Example Swedish: Jag har en bokning i mitt namn.
table.Example English: I have a booking in my name.
Is breakfast included in the price?

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: When asking for something in a hotel, short polite questions work well: “Har ni ...?” “Kan jag få ...?”

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Ja, och här är din nyckel.
dialogue.english: Yes, and here is your key.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Practice saying you have a booking.
Ask if breakfast is included.
Ask politely for a key or room number.
Read the check-in dialogue aloud.

vocabulary.exampleSwedish: Jag har en bokning i mitt namn.
vocabulary.exampleEnglish: I have a booking in my name.
Is breakfast included in the price?

days.title: Review and conversation practice
days.goal: Review real-world Swedish from shopping, weather, hobbies, invitations, and travel.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: This review day aims to make your Swedish feel more social and practical through longer spoken combinations.

table.Example Swedish: Vi har ett kort samtal på svenska.
table.Example English: We have a short conversation in Swedish.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Use earlier chunks instead of searching for perfect grammar. A1 fluency grows from reliable phrases used often.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.swedish: Självklart. Vad gör du i helgen?
dialogue.english: Of course. What are you doing this weekend?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Jag ska träffa vänner och kanske resa lite.
dialogue.english: I am going to meet friends and maybe travel a little.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Have a one-minute conversation with yourself or a partner.
Combine invitations, plans, and weather talk.
Ask for slower speech if needed.
Repeat the dialogue until it feels conversational.

vocabulary.exampleSwedish: Vi har ett kort samtal på svenska.
vocabulary.exampleEnglish: We have a short conversation in Swedish.

days.title: Past tense introduction
days.goal: Recognize the idea of past tense and use a few high-frequency examples.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: This is a light introduction to talking about what happened before now, enough for basic A1 conversation.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Start with common past forms as chunks, such as “var” (was) and “gjorde” (did). You do not need all Swedish past-tense rules yet.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Jag jobbade och sedan åt jag middag hemma.
dialogue.english: I worked and then I ate dinner at home.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Say one thing you did yesterday.
Practice “Vad gjorde du igår?”
Use “var” in two personal sentences.
Read the dialogue and replace the activities.

days.title: Talking about yesterday
days.goal: Build short personal stories about yesterday with simple sequence words.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: You will extend past-time talk from isolated sentences to small, connected events.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Use time words like “först” (first) and “sedan” (then) to organize a simple story even if the grammar stays basic.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Först jobbade jag, sedan lagade jag mat.
dialogue.english: First I worked, then I cooked.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Efteråt såg jag en film och somnade tidigt.
dialogue.english: Afterwards I watched a film and fell asleep early.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Tell a three-step story about yesterday.
Use först, sedan, and efteråt in order.
Practice one past activity aloud.
Read the dialogue until you can retell it.

days.title: Future with ska
days.goal: Strengthen future expressions with ska and personal plans.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: You already met “ska.” Today you use it more actively to talk about tomorrow, next week, and intentions.

table.Example English: I am going to travel next week.
We are going to eat soon.
I am going to call later.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: “Ska” is very common for planned future actions: “Jag ska resa nästa vecka.” Keep the following verb in the infinitive.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.swedish: Vad ska du göra nästa vecka?
dialogue.english: What are you going to do next week?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Jag ska resa och träffa familjen.
dialogue.english: I am going to travel and meet my family.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: When are you going to call them?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.english: I am going to call later today.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Say one plan for later today and one for next week.
Keep “ska” + infinitive together.
Ask a future question with “Vad ska du ...?”
Read the dialogue and replace the plan.

vocabulary.exampleEnglish: I am going to travel next week.
We are going to eat soon.
I am going to call later.

days.title: Writing short messages
days.goal: Write very short messages, reminders, and practical notes in Swedish.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: This lesson helps you turn spoken Swedish into short written communication used in everyday life.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Short messages often omit extra words. Clear, simple Swedish is better than trying to sound advanced.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Ett kort meddelande: “Jag blir sen idag.”
dialogue.english: A short message: “I will be late today.”

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Write a two-line message in Swedish.
Say that you are late or coming soon.
Finish with a simple closing if you want.
Read your written message aloud once.

days.title: Reading simple texts
days.goal: Read short beginner texts and identify the main idea.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: Today is about reading tolerance: understanding enough without translating every single word.

table.Example Swedish: Det finns ett okänt ord här.
table.Example English: There is an unknown word here.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: When reading, focus on known anchors such as names, places, time words, and common verbs before worrying about every detail.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Inte varje ord, men jag förstår huvudidén.
dialogue.english: Not every word, but I understand the main idea.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Den handlar om en familj i Stockholm.
dialogue.english: It is about a family in Stockholm.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Read a short section without stopping at every unknown word.
Find the topic, place, and time in the text.
Write one English sentence about the main idea.
Read the dialogue and keep a calm reading pace.

vocabulary.exampleSwedish: Det finns ett okänt ord här.
vocabulary.exampleEnglish: There is an unknown word here.

days.title: Listening-style practice
days.goal: Train yourself to catch key words in simple spoken Swedish.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: Even without audio, you can practice listening strategy by reading dialogues, pausing, and predicting meaning.

table.Example Swedish: Försök vara lugn när du lyssnar.
table.Example English: Try to stay calm when you listen.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: In listening, you rarely hear every word perfectly. Focus on key items such as names, verbs, time words, and familiar chunks.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.english: A little, but I hear the key words.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Read the dialogue once silently and once aloud.
Underline the key words you catch first.
Retell the main idea in English or simple Swedish.
Do not panic if some words are unclear.

vocabulary.exampleSwedish: Försök vara lugn när du lyssnar.
vocabulary.exampleEnglish: Try to stay calm when you listen.

days.title: Speaking test practice
days.goal: Practice typical A1-style speaking prompts about yourself and everyday life.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: This lesson pulls together the whole course into short oral answers like those often used in beginner exams or interviews.

table.Example English: Try to ask a question back.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: A good A1 answer is short, clear, and complete. One or two solid sentences are better than a long broken answer.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Jag heter Shool. Jag kommer från Indien och jag bor i Finland.
dialogue.english: My name is Shool. I come from India and I live in Finland.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: What do you do in your free time?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Jag läser, tränar och lär mig svenska.
dialogue.english: I read, exercise, and learn Swedish.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Answer five common A1 questions aloud.
Keep each answer to one or two sentences.
Add one question back to the other person.
Repeat weak answers until they are smoother.

vocabulary.exampleEnglish: Try to ask a question back.

days.title: A1 grammar review
days.goal: Review the main grammar patterns from the course in one place.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: This day is for noticing the patterns you already use: word order, negation, questions, modal verbs, and simple time reference.

table.Example Swedish: Gör om meningen till en fråga.
table.Example English: Turn the sentence into a question.
The negation “inte” often comes after the verb.

table.Example Swedish: Det här är en användbar regel.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: The point of review is not to memorize grammar terms. It is to make your most useful patterns faster and more reliable.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: What do you need to review the most?

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Choose three grammar patterns that still feel weak.
Write one example sentence for each.
Read them aloud and correct them if needed.
Use the dialogue as a quick self-check prompt.

vocabulary.exampleSwedish: Gör om meningen till en fråga.
vocabulary.exampleEnglish: Turn the sentence into a question.
The negation “inte” often comes after the verb.

vocabulary.exampleSwedish: Det här är en användbar regel.

days.title: Full A1 revision
days.goal: Review the whole course through self-introduction, everyday tasks, and short conversations.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: This is the final full revision day before the last test lesson. Try to use as much Swedish as possible.

table.Example Swedish: Jag känner mig mer säker nu.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Revision works best when you actively produce language: speaking, writing, and answering prompts from memory.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Jag känner mig mer säker, men jag behöver fortfarande repetition.
dialogue.english: I feel more confident, but I still need revision.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.swedish: Det är normalt. Du gör framsteg.
dialogue.english: That is normal. You are making progress.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Do a full self-introduction with extra detail.
Roleplay a café, shop, and travel situation.
Write five sentences about yesterday and tomorrow.
Mark the last vocabulary items that still feel weak.

vocabulary.exampleSwedish: Jag känner mig mer säker nu.

days.title: Final A1 test and next steps
days.goal: Check your A1 foundations and prepare a clear path for continuing after the course.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: The goal today is not perfection. It is to confirm that you can handle basic Swedish in common beginner situations and know what to practice next.

table.Example Swedish: Vad är nästa steg för mig?
table.Example English: What is the next step for me?
I want to continue with Swedish.
I am going to practice every day.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: A1 is about simple communication: introducing yourself, asking and answering everyday questions, and surviving common real-life situations.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Jag vill fortsätta och öva varje dag.
dialogue.english: I want to continue and practice every day.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Introduce yourself, describe your day, and make one future plan.
Ask and answer ten common A1 questions.
Write a short message and a short past-tense summary.
Choose your next step: more listening, more speaking, or starting A2.

vocabulary.exampleSwedish: Vad är nästa steg för mig?
vocabulary.exampleEnglish: What is the next step for me?
I want to continue with Swedish.
I am going to practice every day.
